subtitle: Lesson 12 · Quantum Error Correction Basics

steps.label: Bit-flip code fixes X, blind to Z. Phase-flip fixes Z, blind to X
steps.sub: Neither alone is a complete solution

steps.label: Shor's insight: concatenate them
steps.sub: Phase-flip code as the outer code, bit-flip code as the inner code

steps.label: Each of the outer code's 3 blocks gets its own inner code
steps.sub: Each block's qubit becomes 3 physical qubits of a bit-flip code

steps.label: 3 outer blocks × 3 inner qubits per block = 9 qubits

eyebrow: Why this covers an arbitrary single-qubit error

steps.label: X error on one of the 9 qubits
steps.sub: The inner bit-flip code covering that block catches it, before it reaches the outer layer

steps.label: Z error on one of the 9 qubits
steps.sub: It flips that whole inner block's phase; the outer phase-flip code catches it at the block level

steps.label: Y error (both X and Z, same qubit)
steps.sub: The inner code fixes the X part, the outer code fixes the Z part — independently, simultaneously

steps.label: 1995: the first proof QEC was possible at all
steps.sub: No-cloning and continuous errors don't actually prevent correction from working

eyebrow: Why real hardware doesn't use this code

steps.label: 9 qubits per logical qubit sounds modest
steps.sub: Far better than a high-distance surface code's thousands — but there's a catch

steps.label: Correction power is capped at exactly 1 error
steps.sub: Scaling up means more concatenation levels, growing cost exponentially

steps.label: Doesn't match real hardware's local connectivity
steps.sub: Superconducting and trapped-ion qubits need nearest-neighbor-only wiring

steps.label: Its importance is historical and pedagogical
steps.sub: It proved the concept — it isn't what a real fault-tolerance roadmap uses
